title: Girls in secondary school: female gross enrollment ratio 2000–2024 (world and three regions) and Bangladesh's female stipend program

facts.text: The gross enrollment ratio compares the number of students enrolled in secondary school, whatever their age, with the number of people of official secondary-school age.
For the world, the female secondary gross enrollment ratio rose from 56.9 in 2000 to 77.1 in 2024.
In South Asia, the ratio for girls rose from 40.6 in 2000 to 78.2 in 2024, the largest rise of the regions in the chart (37.6 points).
South Asia's ratio for girls was below the world figure in 2015 (73.2 against 74.4) but above it in 2020 (76.7 against 75.9).
In Sub-Saharan Africa, the ratio for girls nearly doubled, from 22.7 in 2000 to 44.5 in 2024, but it stayed the lowest of the regions shown in every year.
In East Asia and the Pacific, the ratio for girls rose from 60.9 in 2000 to 92.5 in 2024, the highest of the regions shown in every year.
Starting in 1994, Bangladesh ran a nationwide program that paid a stipend and school fees for girls in grades 6 to 10 in rural areas.
To keep the stipend, a girl had to attend at least 75% of school days, reach a minimum level in her studies, and stay unmarried.
The program aimed to get more girls to enroll in and finish secondary school and to raise the age at which girls marry.
A World Bank study found that the stipend program greatly increased girls' secondary schooling but had no clear effect on boys' schooling.
Each extra year the program ran in an area raised the school enrollment of girls aged 11 to 18 by 12 percentage points.
In Bangladesh, girls' secondary school enrollment rose from 39 percent in 1998 to 67 percent in 2017.
The stipend program helped Bangladesh reach equal numbers of girls and boys in secondary school.
In 2017, 42 percent of girls in Bangladesh dropped out of secondary school before finishing.
